dedupe_keys.name: three us rural hospital closures in 2015 and what they meant for access to care

description: This case study examines what happened to access to care in three rural communities in the United States whose hospitals closed in 2015: Mercy Hospital in Independence, Kansas, Parkway Regional Hospital in Fulton, Kentucky, and Marlboro Park Hospital in Bennettsville, South Carolina. It was produced by the Kaiser Commission on Medicaid and the Uninsured with the Urban Institute and published in July 2016 as an issue brief, free to read online. For each closure the authors held 6 to 8 interviews with nearby hospitals, health centres, health plans, public officials and business leaders, reviewed public material and spoke to rural health experts; two hospitals were in states that had not expanded Medicaid and one in a state that had. Coverage is three towns in three states. Caveats: the evidence is qualitative and from shortly after the closures, and three cases cannot represent all rural closures. The brief found that ageing, poor and shrinking populations, high uninsured rates, a Medicare and Medicaid payer mix, ageing facilities and owners' decisions drove the closures; that closures reduced access to care, especially emergency care; that health professionals left and specialty access worsened; and that elderly and low-income residents faced transport barriers and delayed or went without care, so new care models and regional planning are needed. Simulation uses: qualitative evidence on service withdrawal for rural healthcare access and capacity models. Related records: the national studies of rural hospital closures (case_study-us-rural-hospital-closures-acute-post-acute-care and case_study-us-rural-hospital-closures-surgical-quality-access) measure the effects quantitatively.
